# The Architect's Role {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Everyone designs who devises courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones."*
>
> — Herbert A. Simon, *The Sciences of the Artificial* (1969) [@Simon1969SciencesArtificial]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Herbert Simon defined design through the course from a
present situation to a preferred one. The definition places problem choice,
abstraction, boundaries, and product tradeoffs inside the technical work.
Automation can contribute substantially to that course. The architect's
technical contribution lies in shaping the course into a coherent system and
deciding which design should advance.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
If a capable AI-assisted design system can formulate studies, generate
artifacts, search design spaces, run tools, interpret failures, and recommend
a design, what technical work do architects still contribute?
:::

Grant the strongest premise in this book. AI systems can help formulate a
study, propose mechanisms, generate artifacts, search a large design space,
operate tools, interpret failures, and prepare a technical recommendation. A
capable system may also coordinate predictors, generators, optimizers,
verification tools, and specialist components across a long design study.
Nothing in this chapter depends on preserving a protected set of tasks that
only people can perform.

The architect's role is not whatever automation has failed to absorb. It is a
positive technical role. Architects frame the problem, choose the abstractions
and system boundaries, compose components and disciplines into one feasible
design, interpret disagreement and missing evidence, and decide which
uncertainties a product can carry. They design both the system and the process
that designs alongside them.

This role exists even when every component works as intended. A model can
optimize a network link against the objective it was given, a compiler can
validate a lowering path, a verifier can return a counterexample, and a
physical-design flow can close timing. The architecture problem remains
whether these results describe one product under one consistent set of
workload, software, interface, memory, power, package, and product
assumptions.

The chapter therefore moves from capability to commitment. It first separates
the assessment of the AI-assisted program from the decision to advance a
particular architecture. It then develops the architect's technical work in
problem framing, abstraction, component choice, cross-layer integration, and
interpretation. Only after that work is visible does it address bounded
commitment and the responsibility that continues when conditions change.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Separate an AI program assessment from an architecture commitment.
- Frame an architecture problem whose workload, software path, system
  boundary, constraints, and decision remain coherent as AI and tools act.
- Choose abstractions, methods, components, interfaces, and checks that fit
  the technical problem rather than merely the available automation.
- Integrate specialist results across software, ISA, microarchitecture,
  memory, implementation, package, power, and product concerns.
- Interpret disagreement and uncertainty, make a bounded design commitment,
  and state what later evidence must reopen it.
:::

## Begin with a Capable AI-Assisted Design System

A weak account of the architect's role begins with a list of tasks that current
models cannot perform. That account expires as capability improves. A stronger
account begins with the complete design system and asks which technical
decisions give its work architectural meaning.

Suppose the system can translate a product ambition into candidate studies,
retrieve relevant project knowledge, select or coordinate methods, generate
software and hardware artifacts, run compilers, simulators, formal tools, and
physical-design flows, diagnose failures, revise candidates, and present a
recommendation. Each capability can be real without making the composed system
self-defining. Someone must still decide whether the product ambition became
the right architecture problem, whether the component interfaces preserve the
same candidate and assumptions, and whether the recommendation fits the
consequences of implementation.

This distinction is technical rather than ceremonial. An architecture is not
the union of locally successful component outputs. It is a choice of
mechanisms and interfaces that work together under conditions the product
will encounter. The architect supplies that system view while using the
AI-assisted system as a capable design instrument.

The premise also changes what architects design. They choose not only the
candidate system but also the design process that works alongside them. They
decide where a predictor is useful, where generation can safely propose
artifacts, where optimization should search, which tool returns can reject a
candidate, and how disagreement changes the next action. These choices are as
consequential as choosing a cache hierarchy or an interconnect because they
determine which designs the process can discover and which failures it can
see.

## Program Assessment and Architecture Commitment

The assessment and commitment answer different questions. The program
assessment asks whether the complete AI-assisted system improved architecture
work over a credible alternative at acceptable total cost. The architecture
commitment asks whether this design, under this problem framing, abstraction,
system boundary, evidence limit, organizational capacity, and residual risk,
should advance.

The two decisions also require different evidence. The program assessment
needs a matched complete-system comparison. Architecture commitment needs
design evidence that covers the selected system, the relevant operating
conditions, the cross-layer tradeoffs, and the residual uncertainty. A
favorable result in one decision does not supply the evidence required by the
other.

The three program statuses leave different architecture actions open, so none
determines the commitment by itself (@tbl-two-closing-decisions).

| **Program assessment** | **What it means for architecture commitment** |
| --- | --- |
| Supported | AI improved the architecture by at least the declared minimum worthwhile margin within the acceptable total-cost envelope, or reduced total cost by at least the declared margin while architecture quality remained within the noninferiority margin. The architecture may still be refused because the design, evidence, capacity, or residual risk is unacceptable. |
| Unsupported | AI did not show the required incremental benefit. A sound architecture may still be committed on evidence produced by a conventional or human-directed workflow. |
| Unresolved | No AI-contribution claim is justified. The architecture may proceed only if independent design evidence supports it, or it may remain uncommitted while missing work is completed. |

: **Program assessment and architecture commitment remain independent.**
A favorable result on one cannot substitute for a favorable result on the
other. {#tbl-two-closing-decisions tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

Read down from supported to unsupported to unresolved while keeping the second
column independent. A supported program can still produce a design that should
be refused. An unsupported program can still leave a sound architecture
supported by conventional work. An unresolved program permits no AI
contribution claim and requires the design to stand on independent
architecture evidence. The rows separate how the work was performed from
whether this design should advance.

Reviewability supports both decisions and replaces neither. A well-documented
study can still show that AI added no value. A reviewable design can still be
too risky to commit. Conversely, a useful architecture is not evidence that AI
improved the process that produced it.

The current Lighthouse state makes the separation concrete. Its AI program
assessment is unresolved. Its implementation evidence is also unresolved. The
missing implementation evidence requires refusal of the current
array-and-interface freeze. The unresolved program assessment independently
prevents a claim that AI improved the work. The freeze refusal is not a
permanent rejection of the 32 by 32 candidate or the moonshot. The reference
candidate remains available for the implementation-readiness study.

## Frame the Architecture Problem

Architects do not enter only after a search finishes. Architecture begins
before the candidate set exists and continues after a local result looks
clean. The technical contribution lies in deciding what the system is, which
relationships matter, and which consequences the study must expose. Architects
also create or revise the mechanisms, interfaces, abstractions, and fallback
choices that make specialist results one coherent system. AI may participate
in that work, but the architecture question remains whether those pieces form
a feasible system that meets the product obligation.

Architects also help compose the AI-assisted workflow around that decision.
They determine which method may propose a change, which tool can measure the
relevant property, which check can stop a candidate, and which role resolves
disagreement among returned results. Those choices shape what the study can
observe and which conclusions it can support.

The Lighthouse prompt illustrates the first distinction. A prompt can state an
ambition, but an ambition is not yet an architecture problem. “Design a
low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR
workload” leaves open the representative workloads, supported software path,
product boundary, alternative designs, operating conditions, acceptable
tradeoffs, and decision to be made. Adding more words to the prompt does not
necessarily resolve those choices. Framing turns the ambition into a
challengeable technical question.

The framed problem also determines what the AI-assisted design system must
contain. A study about array utilization may need a cycle-level model and a
mapping search. A decision about freezing the array and its software-facing
interface must also expose compiler and runtime behavior, memory traffic,
implementation feasibility, subsystem power, and the consequences of later
change. The question determines the necessary abstractions and instruments,
not the other way around.

The judgments in @tbl-architect-technical-judgments describe the chapter's
technical spine. They can be informed by models, tools, and specialists, and
they may be distributed across an architecture team.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem choice and reframing | Is the stated problem still the one the product needs solved? | The task is not merely to maximize array utilization. It is to decide whether an implementation-facing compute and software interface meets the mobile XR obligation. |
| Abstraction | Which details can be simplified for this decision, and which must remain visible? | A cycle-level array model can compare mappings locally, but it cannot hide compiler behavior, memory traffic, physical timing, or the 3\ W subsystem boundary from a freeze decision. |
| System boundary | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet? | Array dimensions and dataflow cannot be separated from the runtime, interconnect, memory, energy, and implementation path they require. |
| Architecture synthesis | Do the mechanisms, interfaces, software path, implementation choices, and containment provisions form one feasible system? | The array, compiler and runtime interface, memory path, 3\ W constraint, and fallback behavior must form one implementable subsystem rather than separate local wins. |
| Missing constraints | What has the formulation, representation, objective, or tool path left out? | Representative workloads, interface cost, subsystem power, implementation feasibility, reliability and security properties, and containment remain open obligations. |
| Cross-layer tradeoff | Which feasible point best serves the product when objectives conflict? | Performance, energy, programmability, reversibility, schedule, and review burden must be composed rather than delegated to separate optimizers. |
| Mechanism and consequence | Does the proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens if it is wrong? | The failed directional shape-and-mapping explanation cannot support transfer. A wrong freeze could harden a poor software contract and create costly RTL and physical rework. |
| Commitment under uncertainty | Are the remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting with the available organizational capacity? | The missing implementation-facing tests block the current freeze. The absent matched comparison independently leaves the AI program test unresolved. |

: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** The
architect chooses the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before
deciding whether to commit. {#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

Read down from problem choice, abstraction, and system boundary to the work of
forming one feasible system. The middle rows expose missing constraints and
compose cross-layer tradeoffs that separate specialist results cannot settle.
The final rows ask whether the proposed mechanism and remaining uncertainty
support commitment. The Lighthouse column turns each judgment into a concrete
system consequence. Together the rows describe architecture creation and
technical synthesis, not approval after the design is complete.

## Choose Abstractions, Components, and Constraints

An abstraction is a technical choice about which details must remain visible
for a decision and which can be simplified without changing it. The same
candidate may be represented as an instruction mix, a dataflow graph, a
cycle-level model, synthesizable RTL, a floorplan, or a thermal model. None is
the architecture by itself. Each exposes some relationships and suppresses
others, so the architect chooses the representation whose omissions are
acceptable for the action under review.

This choice determines the rest of the design system. Predictors should model
properties that are expensive to measure but regular enough to learn.
Generators should propose artifacts whose syntax and interfaces can be
checked. Optimizers should search variables with explicit legal regions and
meaningful objectives. Compilers, simulators, formal tools, synthesis,
place-and-route, and physical checks should enter where their observations can
change the decision. The architect may use all of them, but does not assume
that adding components improves the composed system.

The public debate around AlphaChip, a reinforcement-learning method for macro
placement, supplies a concise component-versus-system example
[@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement]. A placement
method can produce strong candidate floorplans quickly. That capability does
not select the product floorplan on its own. The larger architecture and
implementation system still determines the block boundaries, macro set,
timing and power constraints, comparison basis, routability and signoff
checks, and whether the resulting placement serves the chip. A capable
component performs real design work while remaining one component of a larger
technical decision.

Architects also choose how these components interact. They decide which state
crosses an interface, which component may revise it, which tool return blocks
progress, and whether two apparent checks share the same assumptions. In this
sense, architects design both the system and the process that designs
alongside them. The process is not overhead. Its topology changes the
candidates that can be proposed, the properties that can be observed, and the
errors that can survive.

### Making Missing Constraints Reviewable

Some of the most important constraints first appear as expert judgment rather
than a field in a schema. This is *tacit knowledge*, the practical knowledge
that people use but cannot always state completely
[@Polanyi1966TacitDimension]. A compiler specialist may know that a proposed
instruction has no efficient lowering in the supported toolchain. A physical
designer may recognize that a placement heuristic is unsafe for a particular
power-grid geometry, bump pattern, simultaneous-current profile, and
decoupling plan. A product architect may know that a small tail-latency change
crosses a visible XR threshold even when average performance improves.

AI can help locate, compare, and organize these judgments. It cannot make them
authoritative merely by writing them down. The pattern in
@fig-tacit-extraction-bridge keeps validation between elicitation and project
state.

![**Reviewing domain knowledge before using it.** A model can help elicit and organize domain knowledge, but a named domain expert must validate constraints, assumptions, and rejection conditions. Conflicts, expiration, or new evidence require another review rather than a silent overwrite.](images/F11b-tacit-extraction-bridge){#fig-tacit-extraction-bridge width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram showing domain knowledge passing through AI-assisted elicitation and domain validation before entering represented study state, with conflict, expiration, and new evidence returning the record for revalidation."}

Read the figure from left to right. Situated domain knowledge enters a
model-assisted elicitation step that can organize documents, interview
material, assumptions, and contradictions. A named domain expert then
challenges each proposed entry and approves, rejects, or qualifies it. Only
the validated portion enters the represented study state as a constraint,
assumption, rejection check, or validity condition. The blocked direct path
makes the authority boundary explicit, while the return path sends conflicts,
expired conditions, and new evidence back for revalidation. Elicitation can
make a judgment inspectable, but it cannot make the judgment authoritative.

Consider a senior physical designer's rule against placing two high-current
macros on the same power stripe. The geometry and peak-current basis become
project state, the applicable current threshold becomes an environment
constraint, and a floorplan check can reject a violating candidate. The
designer may still need to judge which macros justify the routing cost of
separation. Every retained part needs its source, scope, owner, and
revalidation condition. A change to the power-grid template must reopen the
rule rather than leave it in force as timeless expertise.

The broader lesson is not that every expert intuition should become a formal
rule. It is that a consequential constraint must be visible enough for the
design system to preserve its scope and for another expert to challenge it.
An unrecorded constraint can be optimized away. An overgeneralized constraint
can reject good designs. The architect decides which knowledge becomes model
state, an environment constraint, a rejection check, or a judgment that still
requires specialist review.

## Integrate Across Layers and Disciplines

A candidate becomes an architecture only when its mechanisms and interfaces
work together across the layers that determine product behavior. For the
Lighthouse, this means connecting the XR workload and algorithms to the
compiler and runtime, instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture,
memory hierarchy and interconnect, RTL, physical design, package, power and
thermal limits, verification, and the user-facing product obligation. A local
improvement at one layer has no architectural value if another layer cannot
use or implement it.

Search can find useful candidates and approximate a tradeoff frontier.
Choosing a point on that frontier is a different act. A wider network link may
improve camera-ingest latency while raising switching activity and routing
pressure. A narrower link may save dynamic power while increasing queueing or
software scheduling sensitivity. Some designs may improve both objectives
before the true tradeoff appears. The architect does not assume conflict in
advance. The architect determines which objectives, constraints, operating
conditions, and product consequences make one feasible point preferable to
another.

Finding the frontier is a search problem. Choosing a point on it commits the
product. That choice includes effects that no one optimizer may represent,
such as software turnover, difficult-to-reverse interfaces, verification
capacity, package constraints, field containment, or a user-experience
threshold. A weighted objective can encode a declared tradeoff, but it cannot
decide whether the weights still represent the product.

The architecture role composes specialist judgments rather than replacing
them. A compiler lead may establish whether a lowering path supports an
instruction. A verification lead may establish whether a property passed
within its stated scope. A physical-design lead may establish timing, power
delivery, or routing results. A product lead may define a workload or battery
obligation. The architect determines whether those results address one
coherent system decision and whether an interface between them remains
unexamined.

This is also where the organization of the AI-assisted system becomes an
architecture choice. The study can delegate work broadly without allowing the
candidate identity, assumptions, or decision basis to disappear between
components. @fig-architect-owned-boundary shows the relationship between
delegated technical work, the instruments that support review, and the
architectural decisions that span the complete study.

![**Delegated work and assigned responsibility.** Within a defined study, models, tools, checks, and specialists may assist with problem framing, representation, method choice, tool work, result interpretation, and decision preparation. Named roles remain responsible for scope, abstraction, evidence standards, automation authority, exceptions and waivers, final approval, ownership transfer, and reopening.](images/F11a-architect-owned-boundary){#fig-architect-owned-boundary width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture study containing several kinds of delegated assistance, an architectural claim for review, supporting instruments, and a full-width band of assigned responsibilities."}

Read the figure from top to bottom. The upper region places AI systems, tools,
and specialists across the architecture capabilities the study requires, from
framing through decision preparation. The center groups the design question,
applicable conditions, supporting and conflicting results, and known limits.
Comparisons, checks, replay, iteration, and the study record support that
review without becoming the decision owner. The lower band keeps scope,
abstraction, evidence standards, automation limits, exceptions, final
decisions, transfer, and reopening visible across the complete study.

The figure's central lesson is that delegation changes who or what performs
the work, while integration preserves one architecture question across that
work. The lower band is not a claim that architects manually perform every
step. It identifies the cross-cutting choices that keep locally valid results
from becoming an incoherent system.

## Interpret Results and Disagreement

An architecture result can be numerically correct while its explanation is
wrong. @sec-running-the-loop produced a local no-change outcome and a failed
mechanism explanation. The architect preserves both. The score constrains the
local candidate ranking and technical recommendation under the tested
conditions. The failed explanation blocks transfer based on that mechanism.

This distinction matters because commitment extends beyond the measured
quantity. A mechanism supports predictions about changed workloads, software,
interfaces, or implementation. When it fails, the architect must narrow the
claim, request a discriminating test, or refuse the transition that depends on
it. Fluency, agreement among components, or a clean trajectory does not repair
the missing causal support.

Two automated reviewers may share a common source, model family, retrieval
path, or specification error. Their agreement can corroborate a result without
constituting an independent check. A materially different observation path or
instrument, together with knowledge of correlated failures where available,
is what reduces the shared assumption. The architect decides whether the
remaining dependence is acceptable for the action under review.

Disagreement is therefore useful information rather than a vote to be
suppressed. A predictor and a simulator may disagree because the candidate
left the predictor's training region. A simulator and an RTL check may disagree
because the modeled interface differs from the implemented one. Two physical
tools may disagree because their extracted parasitics or process conditions
differ. The architect asks which assumption separates the results, which
instrument can observe it, and whether the decision can wait for that test.

Consider a coherence verifier that returns a counterexample against a declared
blocking property while the software model treats the same execution as legal.
The proposing system may not weaken the property, remove the failing workload,
or recast the counterexample as a pass. The first technical question is whether
the property and software model encode the same product contract. If they do,
the candidate fails. If they do not, the architecture problem must be corrected
and both paths rerun. The disagreement exposes a system-interface error that
neither local score can settle.

Interpretation also connects a result to consequence. A failed mechanism
explanation may leave a local ranking intact while blocking transfer to a new
workload. A timing pass may support one corner while leaving a power-delivery
failure open. A clean formal proof may establish the declared property while
revealing nothing about whether the property captured the product behavior.
The architect narrows the claim, requests a discriminating test, changes the
design, or refuses the action whose consequence remains unsupported.

Only after the architecture problem, integrated system, and meaning of the
results are clear can a design commitment be made.

## Making and Limiting a Design Commitment

An architecture commitment is a technical system choice. It selects a design
and its interfaces for further implementation, product integration, or
release under stated conditions. Commitment may be reversible during early
exploration and extremely expensive to reverse after an ISA, software
interface, floorplan, package, or mask set hardens. The evidence burden should
rise with that consequence.

The commitment states what design advances, which alternatives were rejected,
which conditions the evidence covered, which uncertainty remains, and what
would invalidate the choice. It does not certify that the design is perfect.
It establishes that the selected system is preferable to the credible
alternatives for the stated product obligation and that the remaining
uncertainty is bounded well enough for the next transition.

Different actions still require different technical authority. Permission to
run a tool does not grant permission to accept its result. Permission to
reject a candidate against a blocking requirement does not grant permission
to weaken that requirement. @tbl-lighthouse-action-rights compresses the
distinction into the four actions that matter for commitment.

| **Action** | **Responsible role** | **Required capacity and boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Propose and measure | Method, environment, and domain specialists | The AI-assisted system may change candidates and run tools inside the declared design space, budget, and evaluator boundary. |
| Accept or reject a technical result | The specialist role responsible for the workload, software, verification, physical, power, security, reliability, or other affected property | The result remains limited to the check's scope. A failed blocking requirement cannot be edited by the proposing system. |
| Recommend the integrated design | System architecture role | Compose cross-layer results, alternatives, disagreement, evidence limits, total cost, and residual risk into one technical recommendation. |
| Commit, contain, or reopen | Authorized architecture and product roles with the required specialist concurrence | Select the design and transition, preserve a usable containment path where possible, and reopen the decision when its conditions no longer hold. |

: **Rights attach to actions, not to a level of automation.** Every
consequential action has a scope, authorized role, capacity requirement, and
path for challenge or reopening. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[22,28,50]"}

The rows move from design work and bounded technical results to an integrated
recommendation and a product transition. Possessing one of these rights grants
none of the others automatically.

The roles must have enough expertise, access, time, and authority to challenge
the work they accept. Otherwise the reviewer becomes a blame-absorbing role
[@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. Reviewers can also exhibit automation bias
[@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias]. Forming an initial view from the
underlying results before reading the automated recommendation can preserve
some independence for consequential choices.

### Residual Risk and Containment

Commitment does not mean that every uncertainty disappeared. It means an
authorized organization decided which remaining risks it could accept, which
it would mitigate, and which blocked the action. Residual risk is therefore a
technical and product decision, not a blank field filled after the design has
already advanced.

A usable residual-risk statement identifies the failure mode, affected scope,
consequence, and basis of uncertainty. It also names the mitigation and its
validating check, the containment or rollback action, and the condition that
will reopen the decision. An exception for a failed or incomplete requirement
must be equally narrow. If no check, operating restriction, or containment
action can still detect or limit the failure, the requirement remains
blocking.

Consider a hypothetical optional Lighthouse vector-turbo mode whose subsystem
power and thermal behavior remain insufficiently characterized. Retaining the
circuitry for later study does not justify enabling the mode. A defensible
exception would require a verified disabled state, an enable path restricted
to an authorized lab or privileged service mode, verified reset, fault, and
access-control behavior, proof that the disabled circuitry does not violate
the base design's functional, timing, power, or security requirements, a named
owner, and an expiration tied to post-silicon characterization. If the
disabled state, isolation, or restricted enable path cannot be validated, the
feature is removed or the design does not advance. The exception does not turn
missing evidence into a pass. At expiration, a new decision must authorize
enablement from new evidence, renew a narrower exception, keep the mode
permanently disabled, or remove it.

Repeated exceptions can make a known failure look like the baseline, the
normalization of deviance described by Vaughan
[@Vaughan1996Challenger]. Expiration and reopening keep a temporary decision
from becoming permanent merely because the system stops reporting it.

### Design Containment Before Commitment

Containment authority matters only when the design contains a credible
technical lever. Depending on the failure, that lever may be a verified
feature-disable path, safe firmware fallback, derating mode, redundant
resource, isolation boundary, rollback path, or refusal to expose the
capability. Some failures have no safe containment short of repair or
replacement. The absence of a credible lever is itself a reason to refuse a
difficult-to-reverse commitment.

Disable mechanisms are not universal insurance. The disabled state must be
verified, the failure must be isolated from required behavior, and the control
path must remain available under the fault being contained. Errata and later
steppings provide established channels for describing and repairing some
silicon defects, but not every erratum has a workaround and not every later
revision fixes it.[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]

[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]: An erratum records a design defect or error that may
cause released silicon to deviate from published specifications, and it may
include a workaround when one exists. Intel's specification update also shows
that a later stepping may fix some errata while others remain unfixed
[@Intel2014CoreMIOUpdate]. The record of an erratum or revision therefore does
not by itself establish containment or repair.

### Capacity to Challenge and Reopen

The organization must be able to challenge the decision it makes. The
question, candidate, conditions, alternatives, results, disagreement, and
current status must remain locatable. Relevant specialists need access to the
artifacts and tools, enough time to inspect them, and the ability to stop or
redirect the transition. The organization also needs the technical and
financial capacity to contain, repair, or retire a committed feature. A gap in
any one of these areas can make an apparently careful commitment impossible
to revisit.

Capacity can erode when automation removes the practice that once developed
it, the irony of automation identified by Bainbridge
[@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. This is not an argument for keeping routine work
manual. It is a reason to keep qualified reviewers in contact with tool
behavior, failed candidates, and cross-layer diagnoses so that the challenge
path remains technically credible.

Opaque external dependencies do not make responsibility disappear. A design
may depend on a vendor model, licensed IP, an access-restricted process design
kit, or a commercial tool that the integrating team cannot inspect fully. The
commitment should identify the versions, vendor evidence, observable checks,
and failures that remain difficult to diagnose. Limits on inspection and
replay become residual risk rather than invisible assumptions.

### The Lighthouse Commitment

The final decision can now be stated without pretending that the missing work
was completed. The current freeze request can be closed while retaining the
candidate for further study (@tbl-lighthouse-commitment).

| **Decision field** | **Current Lighthouse record** |
| --- | --- |
| Problem and candidate | Evaluate a 32 by 32 reference array and its software-facing interface for the XRBench-class mobile XR workload, 64-bit RISC-V hardware-software basis, 3\ W subsystem target, and a pinned low-power mobile implementation process. |
| Architecture action | Refuse the current array-and-interface freeze. Retain 32 by 32 as a reference candidate and continue the implementation-readiness study. |
| Technical basis | Representative workloads, compiler and runtime behavior, mapping, interface and memory cost, subsystem energy and power, RTL behavior, physical implementation, security, reliability, and validated containment remain incomplete. |
| Uncertainty and containment | Treat the missing obligations as blocking unknowns rather than accepted residual risk. Keep the candidate and interface versioned and reversible so downstream work cannot mistake them for a frozen contract. |
| Work required | Exercise the representative workload and software path, measure the complete system boundary, and complete the declared RTL, verification, physical, timing, power-delivery, thermal, security, and reliability checks. Preserve the conditions, failures, cost, and acceptance limits. |
| Reopening condition | Reconsider the freeze when the required coverage, system-boundary measurements, implementation checks, and containment plan are complete, or earlier if a changed product condition makes the candidate or question obsolete. Update the AI program assessment separately through a matched complete-system comparison. |

: **The current action is refusal of the freeze, not rejection of the
candidate.** Missing implementation evidence and an unresolved program
assessment remain visible rather than being converted into permission.
{#tbl-lighthouse-commitment tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Read from the problem and candidate to the architecture action and its
technical basis. The next rows keep blocking unknowns separate from accepted
risk, preserve reversibility, and name the implementation work that could
change the decision. The final row states exactly what would reopen the
freeze. The table records a technical system choice rather than a collection
of approvals.

## Responsibility Continues

The current refusal settles the immediate request but creates continuing work.
Any role receiving that work must receive the decision, its technical basis,
and the conditions that can reopen it. Transfer and field response are
therefore consequences of the commitment record rather than steps that precede
the current decision.

Transferring responsibility means transferring the technical basis, not just the
report. The next role needs enough context to understand what was decided, why
the measurements and checks supported that action, which alternatives failed,
what was waived, and which later condition can overturn the result.
@tbl-ownership-transfer connects each retained object to what must travel and
the failure created when it does not.

| **Transfer object** | **What must travel** | **Failure if omitted** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decision and scope | Architecture question, workload, objective, boundary, candidate, action, and status | The new owner repeats or reverses a decision without knowing what it covered. |
| Technical basis | Represented state, returned results, comparators, uncertainty, mechanism limits, and implementation depth | A bounded result becomes an unqualified claim. |
| Alternatives and dissent | Rejected candidates, failed paths, unresolved objections, and reasons for the selection | Later reviewers cannot distinguish a considered choice from a missing option. |
| Rights and exceptions | Assigned roles, concurrences, permissions, waivers, expiration, and escalation paths | Authority persists after its technical basis or owner has changed. |
| Mitigation and containment | Validated fallback, disable, derating, isolation, rollback, repair, or explicit absence of a credible lever | A named containment right cannot be exercised when a failure occurs. |
| Monitoring and reopening | Signals, thresholds, version mapping, response owner, revalidation triggers, and retirement condition | Changed workloads, software, tools, or field behavior leave a stale decision in force. |

: **Transfer carries the technical argument and the continuing obligation.**
The next owner must know what can invalidate the decision and possess the right
to respond. {#tbl-ownership-transfer tbl-colwidths="[22,43,35]"}

Read down from the decision and technical basis to the alternatives, rights,
mitigations, and later signals that keep the decision current. The middle
column states what the receiving role needs, while the last column exposes the
specific failure caused by omission. A successful file transfer is therefore
insufficient when scope, validity conditions, exceptions, containment, or
reopening authority does not travel with it.

Transfer depth should match consequence and reversibility. Proprietary access
may prevent public reproduction, but the internal transfer must still identify
what only a protected reviewer could inspect.

Consider an explicitly composite example rather than a documented incident. A
thermal predictor is trained and calibrated with aggressive clock gating
enabled across the system, then transferred to a physical-design team for
macro placement. The model artifact arrives, but the clock-gating assumption
and its validated workload envelope do not. The new team treats its predictions
as worst-case coverage, places macros more tightly, and the resulting design
throttles under a field workload outside that envelope. The file transfer
succeeded while the technical basis failed to travel. A responsible transfer
therefore carries the conditions that make a model or result valid, not just
the model, report, or candidate.

### When a Field Result Reopens the Decision

Deployment does not end architecture responsibility. When observed behavior
exceeds ordinary variation, a named role must declare the affected product
scope and use a validated containment lever where one exists. The organization
must investigate the cause, coordinate disclosure under the applicable product
obligations, and reopen the architecture claims and exceptions that the field
result challenges. The resulting action may repair, derate, replace, or retire
the capability.

Failing silicon is high-fidelity evidence that a failure occurred under the
observed conditions. It is not automatically the root cause. The incident
study must still distinguish workload, software, hardware, package,
manufacturing, environmental, and operational explanations.

The Pentium FDIV case discussed in @sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive shows how
a small design omission can become expensive after shipment. The public record
supports missing lookup-table entries and inadequate test coverage. It does
not reconstruct every internal handoff. The durable architecture question is
which role could stop release, who owned customer response, and what evidence
would have reopened the decision before or after the failure became public.

## Open Research Questions

The questions across this book are not a complete research agenda. They are
prompts for forming better questions about what AI-assisted architecture should
make possible, what automated work can support, and what architects must still
be able to judge. This final set widens from individual decisions to the
education, organizations, and discipline that must sustain those judgments.

### Sustaining Architectural Judgment

**How should computer architecture education change when AI-assisted systems
can carry out substantial formulation, implementation, and analysis?**
Students still need enough direct contact with workloads, software, RTL, tools,
and physical effects to challenge a fluent result, but the right mix of manual
practice and assisted work remains open.

**How can organizations test whether responsible architects can still exercise
judgment as automated work volume grows?** The test must cover access,
technical competence, review time, and ability to intervene.

**How much direct practice preserves cross-layer judgment after routine work
is automated?** Computer architecture needs evidence about which experiences
preserve the ability to challenge apparently clean results.

### Authority, Dependencies, and Reversibility

**Which architecture decisions can be delegated without losing accountable
judgment?** A useful answer must distinguish reversible proposals and checks
from commitments that alter interfaces, physical implementation, safety
margins, or deployed behavior.

**How should an architecture commitment treat opaque external dependencies?**
Vendor models, licensed IP, process information, and tools can limit
inspection and diagnosis across organizational boundaries.

**How should the value of containment be priced before the failure is known?**
Disable paths, isolation, derating, rollback, and repair consume resources now
in exchange for future reversibility.

### Defining Progress

**What should count as progress toward an AI-assisted design system that
improves architecture rather than merely automating more work?** The answer
must connect architecture quality, total human and machine cost, reliable
operation, and accountable commitment without collapsing them into one score.

The intended handoff is not a closed list. Readers should form the next
questions, state what would count as an answer, and test whether AI-assisted
architecture work produces systems and decisions worth trusting.

## Closing the Moonshot

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Architecture judgment does not begin where automation ends"}
AI can perform substantial formulation, exploration, implementation, and
analysis. Architects still choose the problem, abstraction, boundary,
cross-layer tradeoff, and consequence that determine whether the resulting
design should be committed.
:::

The two outcomes return separately to the moonshot, as
@tbl-two-closing-decisions requires. The AI program status remains unresolved
because the matched complete-system comparison has not been run. The
array-and-interface freeze is refused because the implementation-facing
evidence is incomplete. That refusal is an architecture decision rather than
an absence of one. It preserves the candidate, names the missing work, and
states what can reopen the question.

If a later assessment supports the AI program, the architect must still decide
whether the selected design and its residual risks justify commitment. If a
later assessment finds no AI contribution, the same architecture may still
advance through a conventional workflow. If the assessment remains
unresolved, no one may turn the absence of a verdict into a success claim.

Architecture 2.0 is a way to use AI for system-and-chip design without reducing
architecture to model output or preserving human work merely because it was
once manual. AI extends the technical work that can be attempted. Architects
create the architecture problem, choose the abstractions and components,
integrate the workload and software path with implementation and physical
consequences, interpret what the results mean, and decide which system should
advance. They also keep that decision valid as workloads, software, tools,
process conditions, products, and field evidence change. That continuing
technical work is what turns capable automation into architecture.
